d.title: An allow-list admits nothing you have not read
d.caption: **A deny-list says which of today's tools you refuse, and the server can add a tool tomorrow.** That new tool arrives in your agent, described by somebody else, callable by a model — and the deny-list admits it silently, because it was written against a list that has changed. An allow-list of names cannot do that. **It is the single most valuable line of configuration in an MCP integration and it costs you a list.** The predicate form is what you want when the allowed set depends on the user, since `get_tools` is called per request.

d.title: Four security facts, and none of them is about the transport
d.caption: **The first row is the one that surprises people and decides whether a server is usable at all:** it acts with its own credentials, so every call uses the same token regardless of which user is talking to your agent. If answers should differ per person — and for anything touching customer data they must — the server needs the user's identity, and most servers do not accept one. **A stdio server is executed code**, which makes it the same trust decision as a dependency: pin it, read it, and never let user input near the command.

d.title: Why a card may not advertise an origin it was not served from
d.caption: **A card is a document telling you where to send your requests, so whoever can serve you a card can redirect your agent's traffic — and its credentials — somewhere else.** The same-origin rule is that redirection defence, which is why the client refuses rather than warns. The example reads as fussiness and is not: `127.0.0.1` and `localhost` are the same machine and different origins. **The fix is always on the serving side** — make the advertised URL describe where the agent is genuinely reachable, which is a deployment concern worth settling before a load balancer finds it for you.

d.title: Three questions a remote boundary raises that a function call does not
d.caption: **The difference between MCP and A2A is the difference between running someone's code and accepting someone's judgement.** You delegate a goal rather than a call, so the remote agent decides the steps — and “find out why this order is late” may mean it reads records you did not intend to expose. **The third row is the one that is easiest to forget:** what comes back is text produced by somebody else's model, entering your model's context, so it is untrusted input in exactly the sense lesson 9.2 means.

d.title: Five situations, and the one place A2A is the wrong answer
d.caption: **Read the bottom branch first, because it is the mistake worth avoiding:** two agents in the same repository that deploy together want a sub-agent, not A2A — one process, one trace, no card, no origin rules, no serialisation. **A2A earns its complexity at an organisational boundary**, where the other side has a different release cadence, different credentials and possibly a different cloud. The distinction in the last two leaves is the useful summary: agent-shaped work is A2A, function-shaped work is MCP.

d.title: What the generated card publishes, from code you already wrote
d.caption: **`to_a2a` derives the card from the agent, which is convenient and publishes more than you may intend.** There is one skill for the agent and one per tool, and each tool's skill carries its full docstring — including the Args section. That is genuinely useful to a caller and it is also your internal parameter documentation, on an endpoint anyone can fetch. **Use `AgentCardBuilder` to build the card deliberately whenever the agent is reachable by someone you have not met**, and read the generated version as an attacker would first.

state: YES - anonymous unless you add it

d.title: The same origin error, from three deployment shapes
d.caption: **The listening address is almost never the public origin, which is why letting the runtime guess fails in exactly the environments that matter.** In a container the agent listens on 0.0.0.0 and is reached through a hostname and TLS it knows nothing about, so a card generated from the socket advertises something no caller can use — and every client refuses rather than retrying. **Set host, port and protocol explicitly, and include `rpc_path` when the agent is mounted under one**, so the card describes where it is genuinely reachable.
